# Explanation and prediction {#sec-explanation-prediction}

In 2017, a group of researchers issued an unusual challenge. The Fragile Families study had followed thousands of American children born around 2000, interviewing their families at birth and at ages one, three, five, and nine: nearly 13,000 variables per family, feeding a literature of over 750 published articles. The challenge: using everything measured through age nine, predict six outcomes at age fifteen, among them the child's grade point average and whether the family would be evicted. One hundred sixty teams tried, wielding every method from linear regression to deep learning, scored on families they had never seen. The best predictions were poor. For the two easiest outcomes the best team explained roughly 20% of the variance; for the other four, between 3% and 6%. A benchmark regression using just four variables chosen by a domain expert came embarrassingly close to the winners [@salganik2020].

Sit with the discomfort for a moment. Hundreds of papers had explained these children's development, or so their titles claimed, yet the same data could not predict those children's lives much better than guessing the average. Something is off in how we think about understanding. For four chapters you have fitted models in order to interpret their parameters: the effect of a policy, the share of variance between schools. In the chapters ahead you will fit models in order to predict, and their parameters may interest nobody. So what is a prediction, and what is it good for when nobody asks for an explanation? And what does predicting well have to do with explaining well? Bring coffee. One formula appears along the way, and I translate it into English on arrival.

## Prediction as a statement about unseen data

A prediction is a statement about data you have not seen. The data may lie in the future but need not: predicting the outcomes of last year's held-out patients, whose files you never opened, is prediction in every sense that matters. What counts is that the model committed itself before the answer was known.

Science has always used prediction in this sense as its court of appeal. A theory implies statements about observations; the observations arrive; the theory survives or does not. You have already done this, in @sec-theory-to-glm, perhaps without noticing. A path model implies correlations, via the tracing rules, and the chi-square test asked whether the observed correlations obeyed. Every claim of absence was a commitment about data not yet consulted. Testing an explanation and checking a prediction are, at bottom, the same act.

Aggregate models make the same move at larger scale. The SIR model of epidemics [@kermack1927] divides a population into susceptible, infected, and recovered persons and predicts a characteristic wave: rise, peak, decline. Real epidemics follow the wave roughly and depart from it instructively, and each departure, from superspreading to waning immunity, forced a better model. The DeGroot model of opinion dynamics [@degroot1974] predicts that people who keep averaging their opinions with their neighbours' will converge to consensus. Look around: no consensus. The model, taken literally, is false, and its failure is informative, since whatever blocks consensus (stubbornness, homophily) is exactly what a better theory must contain. Sociologists in the tradition of @coleman1990 and methodologists like @kkv1994 treat such observable implications as the currency of social theory: a theory that implies nothing checkable buys nothing.

There is a catch, and psychology spent a decade learning it. A verbal theory usually implies far less than its authors think, and testing "the theory predicts a difference in the expected direction" is a feeble hurdle; almost any theory clears it [@yarkoni2022]. Meehl's old complaint applies: predicting *that* it will rain in April is nothing; predicting how many millimetres on which days is science. One diagnosis of the replication crisis is exactly this mismatch between sweeping verbal claims and the timid statistical statements offered as their tests. Real predictive performance, on data the model has not seen, is a discipline that verbal theorizing cannot fake.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.1"}
For each claim, state one concrete prediction it makes about unseen data, and one observation that would embarrass it. (a) The DeGroot model of opinion dynamics. (b) The mediation model of @sec-identification with no direct effect ($X \to M \to Y$ only). (c) "Vocational education helps early careers but hurts late ones" [@forster2016].
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.1"}
(a) Repeatedly interacting groups should drift toward agreement; stable long-run polarization in such groups embarrasses it. (b) The implied correlation restriction $\rho_{XY} = \rho_{XM}\rho_{MY}$ in fresh data; a clearly larger $\rho_{XY}$ embarrasses the exclusion. (c) In a new cohort, the employment gap between vocational and general graduates should be positive at labour-market entry and turn negative around mid-career; a gap that stays flat or grows with age embarrasses the reversal claim. In each case the theory earns credit only in proportion to how easily it could have failed.
:::

## Prediction in its own right

Prediction has a second job that needs no theory at all: sometimes an uncertain forecast is simply better than none, because a decision is waiting. Economists put the distinction in a picture worth keeping [@kleinberg2015]. Deciding whether to carry an umbrella requires only a forecast of rain: the umbrella does not change the weather. Deciding whether to perform a rain dance requires a causal claim: the dance pays only if it makes rain. Umbrella problems are everywhere once you look. Which arriving patients should be fast-tracked? Which defendants will appear for trial? Which households should an anti-poverty programme visit first? Each decision needs to know who, and does not need to know why.

For most of the twentieth century, mainstream statistics in the social and health sciences treated such problems as beneath it. @breiman2001 called out the split in a paper that has aged embarrassingly well. Statistics, he wrote, contains two cultures. The data-modelling culture, which he estimated at 98% of statisticians, assumes a stochastic model and interprets its parameters, validating by goodness of fit. The algorithmic-modelling culture, his 2%, treats nature's mechanism as unknown, seeks any function that predicts well, and validates on held-out data. His warning to the 98% was blunt: conclusions from a fitted model are about the model's mechanism, and "if the model is a poor emulation of nature, the conclusions may be wrong". Twenty years on, his 2% runs the technology sector, and @sec-overfitting and @sec-evaluation teach its methods.

Why would a model built without regard for truth predict better than a model built to be true? @shmueli2010 gives the clean answer: prediction error has two parts, error from bias (the model is wrong) and error from variance (the estimates are noisy), and a deliberately simplified, "wrong" model often wins by trading a little bias for a lot of variance. That tradeoff gets its full machinery in @sec-overfitting. The moral for now: explaining well and predicting well are different objectives, optimized by different models, and neither can be read off from the other.

You can watch the two objectives part ways in a world whose truth we control. The simulation below revisits the exercise-and-symptoms world of @sec-rq-to-interpretation. Exercise 1.5 already had you measure motivation and watch the bias disappear; what changes here is what happens next, since I fit on one half of the data and judge on the other. Exercising still does nothing to symptoms; motivated people still exercise more and feel better.

```{r}
#| label: predict-vs-explain
set.seed(2)
n <- 2000
motivation <- rnorm(n)                           # measured, this time
exercise   <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(motivation))   # the motivated exercise more
symptoms   <- 10 - 1.5 * motivation + 0 * exercise + rnorm(n)
d <- data.frame(symptoms, exercise, motivation)
train <- d[1:1000, ]                             # fit here
test  <- d[1001:2000, ]                          # judge here
m_cause <- lm(symptoms ~ exercise, data = train)
m_pred  <- lm(symptoms ~ exercise + motivation, data = train)
round(c(cause = coef(m_cause)[["exercise"]],
        pred  = coef(m_pred)[["exercise"]]), 2)
rmse <- function(m) sqrt(mean((test$symptoms - predict(m, test))^2))
round(c(cause = rmse(m_cause), pred = rmse(m_pred)), 2)
```

The first pair of numbers are the exercise coefficients: `m_cause` reports $-1.35$, `m_pred` reports $0.00$, and the true effect is zero. The second pair are the root-mean-squared errors on the held-out thousand: `m_pred` misses by 0.97 points on average, `m_cause` by 1.72. Before answering the questions below, be warned that the model names are bait.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.2"}
Extend the chunk above as needed. (a) Which model gives the right answer to the causal question: would prescribing exercise reduce symptoms? (b) Which model should a clinic use to forecast next month's symptom burden, and why? (c) Running `coef(m_pred)` puts motivation at $-1.56$. A policymaker reads this as "boosting motivation lowers symptoms by about 1.5 points". What can the printed output tell her about whether that reading is safe? (d) A principled forecaster refuses to use any variable without causal standing and sticks to `m_cause`. What does the refusal cost, and what does it buy?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.2"}
(a) Neither, as the names stand, but `m_pred` comes far closer: its exercise coefficient of $0.00$ is estimated with motivation, the confounder, held constant, so it recovers the true null effect, while `m_cause`'s $-1.35$ is pure confounding, the left panel of @sec-rq-to-interpretation's simulation compressed into one number. The name `m_cause` is the bait: feeding a regression only the policy variable does not make its coefficient causal. (b) `m_pred`, by a wide margin (0.97 against 1.72), because forecasts are judged on held-out error and motivation carries real signal about symptoms whatever its causal role. (c) Nothing. Her reading happens to be right in this simulation, since the data-generating line gives motivation a real effect of $-1.5$, but the output gave her no way to know that: the same software prints a causal effect ($-1.56$ for motivation) and a confounded artefact ($-1.35$ for exercise in `m_cause`) with equal confidence. Which coefficients have causal standing is settled by design and assumptions, never by the fit. (d) The refusal costs predictive accuracy, 1.72 against 0.97 here, and buys nothing: the umbrella does not care why it rains, and a forecaster restricted to causes is simply a worse forecaster.
:::

The habit of checking prediction pays off even inside ordinary explanatory research, which is the pragmatist's case made by @verhagen2022. Prediction is cheap: any fitted model, including the humble regressions of @sec-theory-to-glm, can be asked to predict, yet in six flagship journals of economics, sociology, and political science, fewer than 5% of abstracts even mention it. He calls the missing ingredient predictive consciousness: knowing whether your celebrated model captures 50% of the outcome's variation or 0.1%. It can be either, at the same $p$-value. Checking per group is more revealing still: a famous mortgage-discrimination analysis fits White applicants well and non-White applicants far worse, a fact invisible in its coefficient table and consequential for every conclusion drawn from it. And @yarkoni2017 close the circle with an unsettling identity: $p$-hacking, the fishing of @sec-rq-to-interpretation, is just overfitting performed by hand, "procedural overfitting". The machine learner's remedies, holding out data and penalizing flexibility, are safeguards for explainers too.

## One decision, two questions

A hospital's appointment book leaks money. Some booked patients never show up; the slot stands empty while another patient waits weeks for it. So the hospital builds a model that flags likely no-shows, and staff call just those patients with a reminder. Look closely at what this decision involves. It needs a forecast: which patients, left alone, would skip? And it touches the world: a phone call can change whether a patient comes.

@kleinberg2015 wrote that observation down as one line of calculus, the formula I promised. A decision-maker chooses an action $X_0$, here calling or not calling, to maximize a payoff $\pi(X_0, Y)$ that also depends on an outcome $Y$, here the patient showing up. The total effect of the action on the payoff splits in two:

$$
\frac{d\,\pi(X_0, Y)}{d X_0} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial X_0}\,(Y)}_{\text{prediction part}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial Y}\,\frac{\partial Y}{\partial X_0}}_{\text{causation part}}
$$

The derivatives are plain sentences wearing notation. The straight $d$ on the left tracks every route by which acting changes the payoff; each curly $\partial$ on the right holds everything else still. The first term is the payoff change with the action, holding the world fixed: calling costs staff time and, when the patient was about to skip, fills an empty slot. Using this term well requires one thing, a good prediction of $Y$, because the action's value depends on what $Y$ will be while leaving $Y$ untouched. This is the umbrella term. The second term is the payoff change through the action's effect on the world: the call itself makes the patient more or less likely to show, and that shift in $Y$ feeds the payoff. Using this term requires a causal estimate of $\partial Y / \partial X_0$. This is the rain-dance term.

Real reminder policies run on both terms at once. Sharp forecasts concentrate the calls where they fill slots, the prediction part. But patients adapt: a clinic that reliably reminds its likely skippers teaches them to wait for the call, and when no call comes they skip more often than before the policy existed, the causation part with an inconvenient sign. A hospital that evaluates its model on forecasting accuracy alone will never see this coming, because the damage lives in $\partial Y / \partial X_0$, a quantity no holdout set contains.

@hofman2021 make the same point at the scale of a research field. Sorting computational social science by what a study estimates and how it is validated, they name the sparsest quadrant integrative modelling: predicting outcomes under interventions and shifting distributions, which is exactly where the two terms of the payoff meet. Their recommendation follows from the split: judge a claim of understanding on both performances, whether its effects are credible and whether its predictions survive out of sample. A model that only explains is a rain dance never tested against the sky; a model that only predicts can collapse the moment a policy changes the world it learned.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.3"}
Classify each decision as mainly a prediction problem (the first term), mainly a causation problem (the second term), or mixed, and name for each the main failure mode of treating it as pure prediction. (a) A judge decides whether to detain a defendant until trial; the worry is flight or a new offence upon release. (b) An agency with limited slots assigns applicants to a job-training programme, aiming to raise employment. (c) A city allocates a fixed team of fire and health inspectors across thousands of commercial buildings. (d) An ICU streams vital signs into a monitor that alerts nurses when a patient appears to be developing sepsis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.3"}
(a) Prediction. Detention works through incapacitation: it keeps a risky defendant off the street no matter why the risk is high, and releasing someone does not cause their riskiness, so the decision turns on forecasting $Y$ accurately. The characteristic failure here runs the other way: demanding a causal account of how defendants become risky before acting, when a plain forecast already improves on unaided judges. (b) Causation. The payoff turns on the treatment effect, on who gains employment because of the training. Ranking applicants by predicted unemployment risk fills the slots with people facing barriers the programme cannot touch; ranking by predicted employability cream-skims people who would have found work anyway. Pure prediction wastes the slots from either end. (c) Mixed. The city needs a forecast of which sites are hazardous, and an inspection changes behaviour, since owners fix hazards because an inspector came. Pure prediction sends the team back to the same incorrigible high-risk sites year after year while ignoring responsive sites that a single visit would fix. (d) Mixed. Detecting incipient sepsis is a forecasting task, but the alert intervenes on clinicians: false alarms breed alert fatigue, and a model with excellent held-out accuracy can then slow the response to true alarms and raise mortality. Accuracy metrics cannot see this failure, because it lives in $\partial Y / \partial X_0$.
:::

## The bitter lesson: language as the extreme case

If you want to see the algorithmic culture's wager pushed to its limit, look at language. For decades, the path to language technology was assumed to run through understanding: formal grammars and hand-built linguistic knowledge. A rival tradition, from the earliest corpus statisticians to the French data-analysis school of Jean-Paul Benzécri, treated language as data for counting rather than a system to axiomatize, and was long dismissed as shallow: surely you need to know *why* a sentence means what it means before a machine can use it. The verdict came in stages. In the 1970s, statistical models beat linguistically informed systems at speech recognition; over the decades that pattern repeated until @sutton2019 distilled it into the "bitter lesson" of seventy years of artificial intelligence: general methods that leverage computation and data eventually beat methods built on human domain knowledge, and the builders' bitterness is part of the story. Large language models are the current endpoint. Their training objective is pure prediction, the next word, with no explanatory ambition whatsoever, and yet they translate, summarize, diagnose, and tutor.

What does the extreme case offer social and health science, beyond a moral? Quite concrete tools, with quite concrete caveats. As *measurement instruments*, language models annotate text (stance, emotion, frames) at a quality approaching trained human coders on many tasks, though unevenly, which argues for using them as one coder on a human team rather than as an oracle [@ziems2024]. As *simulated participants*, they are startling and suspect at once: one large evaluation by Hewitt and colleagues, reported in a position paper reviewing the method, found a model predicting most of the variation in average treatment effects across dozens of preregistered experiments [@anthis2025], yet the same systems compress the variance of human opinion, misrepresent minorities, and may simply be remembering the studies they were trained on [@bail2024; @grossmann2023]. As *agents*, they revive agent-based modelling with actors that talk. The prudent summary: a purely predictive model of human text is a genuinely new scientific instrument, and every use of it re-raises this book's oldest question, namely what assumptions connect this instrument's output to the quantity we care about.

## Two mass collaborations

The Fragile Families Challenge that opened this chapter deserves a closer look, alongside its European successor, because together they are the cleanest measurements yet of how predictable individual lives are.

**The Fragile Families Challenge** [@salganik2020] borrowed machine learning's **common task framework**: one dataset, one holdout, one metric, many independent teams, so that failure cannot be blamed on any single researcher's skill. The borrowing was deliberate, and from a winner. Donoho's history of data science credits this framework, public data, enrolled competitors, and a neutral referee scoring held-out predictions, as "the 'secret sauce' of machine learning", the engine behind decades of steady gains in speech and language systems [@donoho2017]. The challenge turned the same engine on a social-science question. The material was rich by any social-science standard: 4,242 families, 12,942 variables spanning birth through age nine, purpose-built survey data rather than found data. Performance was scored as $R^2$ on held-out families, relative to simply predicting the average. The results, once more, with the numbers in view: the best submissions reached about 0.23 for material hardship and 0.19 for GPA, and 0.03 to 0.06 for grit, eviction, caregiver layoff, and job training. The four-variable expert benchmark was "only slightly worse than the most accurate submission". Two further findings sharpen the picture. The 160 teams' predictions, for all their methodological diversity, agreed with each other far more than any of them agreed with reality; and prediction error concentrated in particular *families*, not particular methods. The authors draw the conclusion carefully: the results "suggest practical limits to the predictability of life outcomes in some settings", and policymakers buying predictive tools for child protection or criminal justice should ask for exactly this kind of evidence before believing vendor accuracy claims.

**PreFer** [@sivak2024] is the designed follow-up, and its design shows a field learning. The task: predict which Dutch residents aged 18 to 45 will have a child in 2021 through 2023, from data through 2020. One outcome, well theorized, with a deliberately short three-year horizon. Two data sources compete. The LISS panel is "wide" in variables: over 30,000, including stated fertility intentions, the kind of subjective variable registers never contain, but with roughly 1,400 outcome-labelled cases. The Dutch population registers are "long" in cases: millions, 1995 through 2023, even the full kinship network, but limited to objective variables. The headline metric is F1, which balances precision and recall on the positive class, chosen because with about one in five positives, raw accuracy flatters models that predict "no child" for everyone. Teams submit runnable methods rather than predictions, fixing a reproducibility weakness the Fragile Families organizers discovered in their own archive. Above all, PreFer converts the earlier puzzle into a decomposition: if prediction fails on the survey but succeeds on the registers, the bottleneck was sample size; if the reverse, the subjective variables were the treasure; if both fail, the unpredictability starts to look like a property of lives rather than of datasets.^[The benchmark paper describes the challenge design; the challenge itself ran in 2024, and its results are reported separately by the organizers (see stulp.gmw.rug.nl/prefer). The joint lesson of this literature so far is consistent: predicting individual life outcomes is far harder than our explanatory confidence suggested.]

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.4"}
(a) In the Fragile Families Challenge, why does the common task method make "low predictability" a conclusion about the phenomenon rather than about the researchers? (b) The best GPA model reached $R^2 \approx 0.19$ against a mean-prediction baseline. A press release announces: "algorithm predicts children's school success". Write the two-sentence correction. (c) Explain why PreFer's organizers chose F1 rather than accuracy, using the base rates given above.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.4"}
(a) One hundred sixty independent teams with free choice of methods all faced the same holdout and the same metric; when the best of them barely beats a four-variable regression, "a better analyst would have done better" loses its plausibility, which was the design's purpose. (b) "The best of 160 competing models explained about a fifth of the variation in GPA, leaving four fifths unexplained; it beat a four-variable regression by a few points. Individual children's outcomes remained largely unpredictable from thirteen thousand variables." (c) With roughly 15 to 22% positives, predicting "no child" for everyone scores about 80% accuracy while identifying no one; F1, which balances precision and recall on the positive class, gives such a model the zero it deserves.
:::

## Pendulums: successes and failures

Fields swing between explanation and prediction, and the swings are instructive.

Macroeconomics swung twice. In the 1970s, its large "structural" models, hundreds of equations of interpretable theory, predicted poorly, and @sims1980 argued for replacing them with frankly atheoretical time-series models that simply let recent data forecast the near future. The forecasting improved; the approach earned Sims a Nobel prize in 2011. And then the pendulum returned: for questions about *policy*, rain-dance questions, forecasting models are silent by construction, and the following generation of economists rebuilt causal credibility with the designs and instruments of chapters 1 and 3, work honoured with its own Nobel a decade later. Both swings were rational. The field learned which of its questions were umbrella questions and which were not.

Prediction has its cautionary tales too. Google Flu Trends estimated influenza incidence from search queries, faster than the official surveillance it aimed to complement, and for a while it worked; then it drifted, at one point overestimating flu prevalence by a factor of two, partly because the search engine and its users kept changing under the model [@lazer2014]. The failure is the mirror image of the Fragile Families lesson: an impressive fit on the past is a statement about the past, and a predictive model deployed in a changing world quietly becomes a model of a world that no longer exists. Meanwhile the quiet successes accumulate without headlines: clinical risk scores triage chest pain, predicted readmission risks schedule follow-up calls, and no one demands that these models explain anything, only that they keep being right.

## What to carry forward

Four ideas from this chapter travel into the machine learning chapters. A wrong model can predict better than the true one, which stops being a paradox once error is split into bias and variance, the subject of @sec-overfitting. A prediction is a statement about unseen data, so evaluation always requires data the model has not touched; @sec-overfitting names the failure, overfitting, and @sec-evaluation shows how to arrange the checking, and how badly things go when you cheat. A decision's payoff has an umbrella term and a rain-dance term, and no accuracy metric can certify the second. And the chain of @sec-rq-to-interpretation never went away: a predictive model answers its question under assumptions, chiefly that the future resembles the training data, and Google Flu shows what their violation looks like. The tools change in the next two chapters. The five questions do not.

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.A"}
A researcher has panel data on adolescents: social media use, sleep, exercise, parental monitoring, and depressive symptoms, over four years. Two goals are on the table. Goal 1: estimate the effect of social media use on depressive symptoms, for policy advice. Goal 2: flag adolescents at high risk of developing symptoms next year, so the school counsellor can reach out.

(a) For each goal, which variables belong in the model, and by what criterion?
(b) For each goal, what is the appropriate way to judge whether the model is good?
(c) The Goal 2 model puts large weight on parental monitoring. A journalist concludes that monitoring causes depression. Explain the error, and what would go wrong if a school acted on it.
(d) Conversely, suppose the researcher uses only the variables with credible causal effects for Goal 2's forecasting task. What is sacrificed, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.A"}
(a) Goal 1: variables chosen by the causal logic of chapters 1 and 3: confounders of use and symptoms must enter, mediators must stay out of the total-effect equation, and instruments or designs must carry the assumptions. Goal 2: anything measurable in advance that improves held-out prediction, including proxies with no causal standing. (b) Goal 1: by the credibility of the design and assumptions, plus uncertainty of the estimate; fit alone proves little. Goal 2: by predictive performance on held-out adolescents, with a metric suited to the base rate and to the costs of misses versus false alarms. (c) Predictors earn their weights by association, and monitoring may be a marker of parents already worried about a struggling child; acting on it causally (discouraging monitoring) could remove a response to risk rather than a cause of it, the umbrella-rain-dance confusion in the wild. (d) Predictive accuracy: causal variables are often few, weak, or hard to measure early, while non-causal markers carry real signal; a forecaster restricted to causes is a worse forecaster, which is Breiman's point in one sentence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.B"}
A team proposes to use a language model to code 40,000 open-ended survey answers about vaccine hesitancy into five categories, replacing two student coders.

(a) Describe a validation design that would justify the substitution, including what quantity you would compute.
(b) Name two failure modes specific to language models that your design should probe, and how.
(c) The model classifies answers written in regional dialect noticeably worse. Which concept from this chapter (and from @sec-rq-to-interpretation) does this instantiate, and what would you do?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.B"}
(a) Have the human coders label a random subsample (stratified over categories and respondent groups); compare model and human labels via agreement statistics such as Cohen's kappa, benchmarked against the two humans' agreement with each other; only substitute if model-human agreement approaches human-human agreement, and keep humans on a continuing audit sample. (b) Training-data contamination and drift: probe by testing on newly written answers the model cannot have seen. Systematic skew, such as sycophantic or majority-flavoured readings of ambiguous answers: probe by comparing error rates across answer types and demographic groups. (c) Differential measurement quality, a construct-validity threat, and a violation of the assumption that the instrument works equally well across units; remedies include dialect-specific validation, human coding for the affected group, or adjusting analyses for known error rates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.C"}
"Since the best Fragile Families models explained only 20% of GPA variance, social science has learned nothing about child development." Write a short assessment (at most 200 words) that engages the strongest version of both sides.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.C"}
A model answer engages both directions. For the provocation: if understanding is measured by out-of-sample prediction, the result is damning, since 750 papers' worth of variables barely beat four chosen by hand, and the shortfall was no one team's fault by design. Against it: explanation and prediction are different targets; a modest average causal effect can be real, replicable, and policy-relevant while individual outcomes stay dominated by idiosyncratic events, so low individual predictability does not refute the causal knowledge. The strong synthesis notes what the challenge actually adds: a measured ceiling, so far unexplained, which theories of development must now themselves explain; a warning for anyone deploying individual-level risk prediction in policy; and a template, extended by PreFer, for finding out whether the ceiling reflects data limits or genuine randomness in lives. "Nothing" overclaims; "business as usual" underclaims; the defensible position is that social science learned something painful and useful about the kind of knowledge it has.
:::
